results.content: I have two questions regarding the calculation of the inter-annotator reliability using Cohen’s kappa. Is it possible to calculate inter-annotator reliability only with reference two one single value of the controlled vocabulary? I have noticed that if only two values of the controlled vocabulary are used, the inter-annotator reliability result is NaN (not a number). Since one tier has 100% “x” and the other 82%, I would expect a strong inter-annotator reliability result, even in the case segmentation differs between the two tiers. The outcome could be quite similar to what you got so far (except maybe for those annotation values that occur only a few times compared to most other values, see e.g. the Limitations section of the kappa Wikipedia page). Anyway, if you want to try that, you could maybe use e.g. the `Tier->Copy Annotations from Tier to Tier` to create 2 new tiers both containing only the value you are interested in (that function has such an option).

results.title: Interobserver agreement issues in radiology - ClinicalKey
results.content: Intra- and inter observer agreement is a critical issue in imaging and this must be assessed with the most appropriate test. Cohen's kappa test should be used to evaluate inter-rater consistency (i.e., inter-rater reliability) for qualitative (nominal or ordinal) variables. Agreement between observers (i.e., inter-rater agreement) can be quantified with various criteria but their appropriate selections are critical. When the measure is qualitative (nominal or ordinal), the proportion of agreement or the kappa coefficient should be used to evaluate inter-rater consistency (i.e., inter-rater reliability). When the measures are quantitative, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) should be used to assess agreement but this should be done with care because there are different ICCs so that it is important to describe the model and type of ICC being used. In radiology, agreement between readers can be analyzed when comparing different imaging techniques or determining presence of a given variable (e.g., imaging criterion). Agreement between readers (inter-rater agreement) can be quantified with various settings but their appropriate selection is critical and depends on the nature of the measurements. When the measure is qualitative (nominal or ordinal), the proportion of agreement or Cohen kappa coefficient should be used to evaluate inter-rater consistency (i.e., inter-rater reliability). A possible error is the use of chi-square test (χ 2 ) that evaluates statistical association between two readers but not a measure of agreement. Although this method is intuitive, it does not take into account agreements that can be obtained by chance alone and that is the essence of the Kappa statistics. The difficulty here is that ICC can measure both agreement and consistency (i.e., association between the measurements performed by each observer). The absolute agreement definition should be selected for test-retest and intra-rater reliability assessment. The ICC is an acceptable summary measure for agreement between continuous data, but it does not give information about the variability of data with the magnitude of measurements. Landis J.R., Koch G.G.: The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Bland J.M., Altman D.G.: Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement. Tipton E., Shuster J.: A framework for the meta-analysis of Bland-Altman studies based on a limits of agreement approach.

results.title: Inter-Annotator Agreement: An Introduction to Cohen’s Kappa Statistic | by Surge AI | Medium
results.content:
Title: Inter-Annotator Agreement: An Introduction to Cohen’s Kappa Statistic | by Surge AI | Medium
You’re tired of grading homework and want to get back to your research, so you decide to build an NLP model that can score your students’ essays as a Pass or Fail for you. In this post, we’ll explain how Cohen’s kappa uncovers disagreements between raters that are obscured by simpler metrics like percentage agreement. As starving aspiring novelists, Alix and Bob were both happy to moonlight as data labelers grading student essays. The problem with simple measures of inter-rater reliability, like the percentage of samples both raters label identically, is that they don’t account for the likelihood that two people would agree by random chance. The raters also rarely disagreed about which essays were good: if Alix passed a student, Bob did too 86 / 94 = 91% of the time. We can fix both these issues by using Cohen’s kappa to measure inter-rater reliability. In this case, it’s not clear which, if any, rater is objectively correct, so we can arbitrarily define this as the number of students Alix passed and Bob failed. * FP is the number of false positives, i.e. the number of students Bob passed and Alix failed. Cohen’s kappa ranges from 1, representing perfect agreement between raters, to -1, meaning the raters choose different labels for every sample. Alix and Bob could easily achieve a Cohen’s kappa of 1 if they were both so lazy they decided to just auto-pass every single essay. A high Cohen’s kappa might also reflect shared inappropriate biases — imagine if Alix and Bob both resented being forced to read Shakespeare in high school and automatically failed anyone who mentioned him. Similarly, negative values for Cohen’s kappa don’t automatically mean that one of the raters is low-quality. In this essay grading example, for instance, Alix might value thoroughness while Bob prefers students who are concise. Even for tasks that require consistency, low Cohen’s kappa values may reflect ambiguous instructions or inherently subjective questions (what makes an essay good anyway?) rather than rater error. (For example, if Alix and Bob gave every essay an A-F grade instead of just pass/fail.).

Title: python - Multi Label Annotator agreement with Cohen Kappa - Stack Overflow
### your communities. ### more stack exchange communities. ##### Collectives™ on Stack Overflow. # Multi Label Annotator agreement with Cohen Kappa. Every document can be annotated with multiple labels. In this example, I have 2 annotators (a and b), and they each label two documents. `from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score. Annotator\_a labels document 1 with labels a, b and c. Annotator\_b labels documents 1 with labels b and c. `ValueError: You appear to be using a legacy multi-label data representation. ## 3 Answers 3. Cohen's Kappa does not support multi-label input. Instead of using Cohen's Kappa, one could use Krippendorff's Alpha. The specific error is due to an unsupported representation of multi-label output (see documentation of `type_of_target` function of sklearn). Even the correct multi-label output you would still get an error since `cohen_kappa_score` does not support multi-label input (see below). In fact, Cohen's kappa *can be applied for multi-class problems only for **exclusive** classes*, and multi label output is by definition non exclusive. What you could do is have a binary classifier for each label and compute Cohen's kappa for each label. If you need a unique number representing agreement you could compute the average kappa over the labels. ## Example: Cohen's kappa for multi label. cohen_dict = {k: cohen_kappa_score(a_dict[k], b_dict[k]) for k in labels}. cohen_dict: {'a': 0.0, 'b': 1.0, 'c': 1.0, 'd': 0.0, 'e': 0.0, 'f': 0.0}. ### how to transform to sequence of sequence to correct multi label representation. Although original Cohen's Kappa statistic does not support multiple labels, there are proposed extensions to address this case. By assigning weights to each label, Kappa values allows one to analyze the contribution of primary and secondary (and potentially more) categories to agreement scores. For details, refer to the Augmenting the kappa statistic to determine interannotator reliability for multiply labeled data points paper. The weighted Kappa mentioned above is still limited to pairs of labelers. ## Your Answer. Thanks for contributing an answer to Stack Overflow!
